title: SignalR transports hubs connection lifetime groups security scaling
concepts: SignalR provides server-to-client and bidirectional real-time messaging over a logical connection. A hub is a high-level RPC-like abstraction for client and server method calls; it is not a durable event log or a guarantee that every message is delivered exactly once. Design reconnect, replay, persistence, and acknowledgement behavior explicitly when messages matter. In ASP.NET Core 11, the .NET client can cancel a non-streaming invocation cooperatively, and the JSON Hub Protocol can serialize C# union types through System.Text.Json.

SignalR negotiates a transport and protocol, then maps client invocations to hub methods. WebSockets is generally the preferred transport when available; Server-Sent Events and long polling provide alternatives. A hub instance is transient per invocation, so application state belongs in a scoped or durable service, not in hub fields. Use IHubContext to send to clients outside a hub invocation.

Connections, users, and groups are distinct: one authenticated user may have multiple connections, and groups are transient routing sets rather than authorization boundaries. Every hub method and group membership change must be authorized against trusted server-side identity and resource data. Treat all client-supplied arguments as untrusted and avoid sending secrets or sensitive information to broad groups. In ASP.NET Core 11, optional token refresh may replace claims in place only when the refreshed principal retains the same SignalR user identity; the connection ID and user-routing identifier do not change.

Horizontal scale-out requires connection affinity or a managed service and a backplane, depending on transport and hosting topology. The Redis backplane distributes messages but does not persist or replay them after outages; Azure SignalR Service manages client connections and scale-out differently. Stateful reconnect can buffer and replay a limited window after short interruptions, but it is not durable delivery.

SignalR stateful reconnect does not provide durable message delivery

Stateful reconnect is available starting in .NET 8 and remains opt-in on both server and client. It acknowledges and buffers a bounded amount of data to smooth short network interruptions; it does not make SignalR a durable delivery system.

ASP.NET Core 11 adds active SignalR authentication refresh support for .NET and TypeScript clients. A refreshed principal updates claims and roles in place while preserving the SignalR user identifier and routing; existing in-flight hub invocations retain the principal they began with.
ASP.NET Core SignalR is not wire/API compatible with classic ASP.NET SignalR. Teach the current ASP.NET Core server and client packages and mention classic SignalR only as migration context.

Automatic reconnect remains opt-in for ASP.NET Core SignalR clients. It establishes a new connection after reconnect and does not replay messages; use stateful reconnect only for its bounded transient-disconnect behavior.

ASP.NET Core 11 adds server-controlled authentication refresh for SignalR connections. The refresh request reauthenticates through the normal endpoint pipeline; the refreshed principal must map to the same SignalR user. An optional OnAuthenticationRefresh callback can reject additional changes but cannot approve a different user identity. Automatic refresh requires a reported token lifetime; failed refresh is surfaced to the client and does not itself close or retry the connection.

ASP.NET Core 11 lets the .NET SignalR client cancel non-streaming InvokeAsync calls by sending a cancellation message. The hub method must declare and observe CancellationToken; cancellation is cooperative, the client task cancels before the server necessarily finishes, and older servers only canceled the local wait. This invocation-cancellation feature is .NET-client-only.
ASP.NET Core 11 supports C# union types through System.Text.Json in the SignalR JSON Hub Protocol. This does not imply support in the MessagePack protocol.

scopeExclusions: Generic authentication schemes, JWT validation, cookie configuration, authorization policy construction, CORS, and antiforgery are taught in dedicated ASP.NET Core security topics.
Browser WebSocket APIs and general HTTP transport semantics are covered in the browser and protocol topics; this manifest covers SignalR transport selection and constraints.
Redis internals, cloud service setup, broker durability, application event design, and distributed presence stores belong to infrastructure and architecture topics.
Client framework integrations beyond the official .NET and JavaScript clients are third-party package APIs and are not enumerated as built-in SignalR features.
